newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Zaire backs U.N. peace plan, Belgium says.
newsitem.headline: Zaire backs U.N. peace plan, Belgium says.

text.p: Zaire has approved a United Nations plan designed to end the crisis in the African state, the Belgian foreign ministry said on Wednesday.
"We are pleased to see that Mr Kamanda has confirmed that his country has approved a five-point United Nations plan...," ministry spokesman Andre Querton told a weekly news briefing.
He said Belgian Foreign Minister Erik Derycke had met his Zairean counterpart Kamanda Wa Kamanda on Monday.

Zaire has accused the regular armies of Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of fomenting an almost five-month-old Tutsi-led rebellion in eastern Zaire and of actively participating in fighting on Zairean soil.
All three countries deny the allegations.
Querton said the U.N. plan called for an immediate end to hostilities and the withdrawal of all foreign troops, including mercenaries.
It also demands a swift and peaceful solution to the crisis through dialogue, the election process and by convening an international peace conference, he said.

It also calls for the national sovereignty and territorial integrity of Zaire and other countries in the region to be respected and urges protection for all refugees and easy access for humanitarian actions.

Querton said a new African summit had been scheduled for March 18-19 in Nairobi with delegations from Kenya, Zimbabwe, Cameroon, South Africa, the Organisation of African Unity and other countries in the region.
Nairobi has already hosted two summits on Africa's latest conflict.

A third summit there had earlier been opposed by Uganda and Rwanda which both feared Kenya's leadership was too close to Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko to be impartial -- a view also supported by rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Kabila is an old-time ally of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni, a former rebel leader accused by Zaire and suspected by Kenya of seeking to carve out an empire for the Tutsi tribe in the region.
Belgium also stressed the vital role of African countries and organisations in the crisis, Querton said, but added that Belgium was aware of human rights violations by both parties in the conflict.
"We have (now) received other witness accounts on major violations of human rights in the region," he said, repeating a call for U.N observers to be sent to the region.
"We believe that Kabila has accepted the principle," he said. "We are in contact with the centre for human rights in Geneva to see how it could be set up."
Querton said many African countries were interested in the initiative by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to try and set up an international humanitarian force.
